evidence.claim: Brick highway remnants trace an earlier journey through Espanola and Bunnell.
evidence.quote: The Dixie Highway-Hastings, Espanola and Bunnell Road (also known as County Road 13 or the Old Brick Road) is a historic section of Old Dixie Highway in Florida.

evidence.claim: Heritage Crossroads is a 98-mile road network centered on Bunnell in northeastern Florida, reaching into Flagler, Volusia and St. Johns counties.
evidence.quote: This network of roads is located in Flagler, Volusia and St. Johns Counties in the northeastern part of the state and is centered at the hub in Bunnell.

evidence.claim: Its roads connect the Old Brick Road at Espanola, Bunnell’s US 1 corridor and the eastward drive on State Road 100 to Flagler Beach.
evidence.quote: It is located at the intersection of Old Brick Road, County Road 13, and County Road 205.

evidence.claim: Designated on November 19, 2008, the scenic highway is presented by Florida’s Department of Transportation as a route through the region’s settlement and travel history.
evidence.quote: Designated: November 19, 2008 FDOT District: 5 Overview The segments of road and the communities that comprise this byway embrace the heritage of the people who built the region.

evidence.claim: The Dixie Highway began as an auto-trail proposal in 1914, promoted by Carl G. Fisher to connect the Midwest and South.
evidence.quote: Dixie Highway was a United States auto trail first planned in 1914 to connect the Midwest with the South.

evidence.claim: It developed into a network of connected roads.
evidence.quote: The final system is better understood as a network of connected paved roads, rather than one single highway.

evidence.claim: At Espanola, highway traffic brought tourists and businesses.
evidence.quote: This highway opened a new tourist trade as well as attracted new residents and businesses, which boosted the economy in the Espanola area.

evidence.claim: Then a new road, now US 1, bypassed the town in 1926, and automobile traffic fell sharply.
evidence.quote: In 1926, a new highway (now U.S. 1) was built from St. Augustine directly to Bunnell and bypassed Espanola.

evidence.claim: The Old Brick Road survives as part of the original brick Dixie Highway.
evidence.quote: This is one of the few extant portions of the original brick Dixie Highway left in Florida.

evidence.claim: Start at Espanola’s Old Brick Road junction, then head toward Bunnell, the network’s hub.
evidence.quote: It is located at the intersection of Old Brick Road, County Road 13, and County Road 205.

evidence.claim: State Road 100 runs eight miles east from Bunnell to Flagler Beach.
evidence.quote: Florida State Road 100 leads 8 miles (13 km) east to Flagler Beach

evidence.claim: Bulow Plantation’s ruins lie on a separate excursion south of SR 100.
evidence.quote: It is three miles west of Flagler Beach on CR 2001, south of SR 100

evidence.claim: Finish inland at Codys Corner, where Dupont Road meets State Road 11 southwest of Bunnell.
evidence.quote: The community is at the intersection of Dupont Road and State Road 11 southwest of Bunnell in Flagler County, Florida.

evidence.claim: 98-mile road network
evidence.quote: Byway Length: 98 Miles

evidence.claim: Bunnell’s US 1 corridor and the eastward drive on State Road 100 to Flagler Beach
evidence.quote: U.S. Route 1 passes through the center of Bunnell as State Street, leading north 31 miles (50 km) to St. Augustine and southeast 18 miles (29 km) to Ormond Beach. Florida State Road 100 leads 8 miles (13 km) east to Flagler Beach

evidence.claim: promoted by Carl G. Fisher
evidence.quote: The prime booster of both projects was promoter and businessman Carl G. Fisher.

evidence.quote: It is located at the intersection of Old Brick Road, County Road 13, and County Road 205.

evidence.quote: This is one of the few extant portions of the original brick Dixie Highway left in Florida.

evidence.claim: Automobile travelers once supported a hotel and camps here.
evidence.quote: Over-night tourists (known as ‘Tin Can Tourists’) prompted the establishment of a new hotel and camps to accommodate these automobile-campers.

evidence.claim: In 1926, the new highway from St. Augustine directly to Bunnell bypassed Espanola, diverting traffic and damaging the local economy.
evidence.quote: In 1926, a new highway (now U.S. 1) was built from St. Augustine directly to Bunnell and bypassed Espanola. This rendered the Dixie Highway route through Espanola obsolete as automobile traffic drastically declined and very few tourists and travelers ventured to Espanola. The economy of Espanola was devastated

evidence.claim: The old road entered the National Register of Historic Places in 2005.
evidence.quote: On April 20, 2005, it was added to the U.S. National Register of Historic Places.

evidence.claim: The Florida Department of Transportation identifies the Old Brick Road as a place to walk, cycle or drive.
evidence.quote: Travelers can hike, bike, or even drive on the “Old Brick Road” segment.

evidence.claim: The Old Brick Road preserves part of the original brick Dixie Highway.
evidence.quote: This is one of the few extant portions of the original brick Dixie Highway left in Florida.

evidence.claim: The ruined sugar mill is built of coquina, a sedimentary rock made of shells.
evidence.quote: contains the ruins of an antebellum plantation and its sugar mill, built of coquina, a fossiliferous sedimentary rock composed of shells.

evidence.claim: Enslaved Africans and African Americans supplied the plantation’s forced labor.
evidence.quote: was operated with the forced labor of enslaved Africans and African Americans.

evidence.claim: Charles Wilhelm Bulow began developing the plantation in 1821, making his enslaved workforce clear land for indigo, cotton, rice and sugarcane.
evidence.quote: The plantation was developed beginning in 1821 by Major Charles Wilhelm Bulow, who acquired 1,892 ha (4,675 acres) on a tidal creek (later Bulow Creek). He had 890 ha (2,200 acres) cleared by the labor of his enslaved workforce for the cultivation of commodity crops: indigo, cotton, rice, and sugarcane.

evidence.claim: The plantation was destroyed in the Seminole War of 1836.
evidence.quote: The plantation was destroyed in the Seminole War of 1836.

evidence.claim: Florida acquired the property and ruins in 1945 and dedicated the historic park in 1957.
evidence.quote: The property and ruins were acquired by the State of Florida in 1945 and dedicated as a State Historic Park in 1957.

evidence.claim: The interpretive center holds original artifacts and exhibits on the plantation.
evidence.quote: The park's interpretive center features original artifacts and exhibits about the Bulow Plantation.

evidence.claim: Shells form the coquina stone used in the ruined sugar mill.
evidence.quote: its sugar mill, built of coquina, a fossiliferous sedimentary rock composed of shells.

evidence.claim: At Dupont Road and State Road 11, Codys Corner takes its name from local farmer Richard Cody, Sr., who named it in 1907.
evidence.quote: Codys Corner was named in 1907 by Richard Cody, Sr., who was a local farmer.

evidence.claim: It was also called Codyville, the name used in the 1932 US Geological Survey.
evidence.quote: In the early days, Codys Corner was also known as Codyville and this is the name it appeared under during the 1932 US Geological Survey.

evidence.claim: By the 1950s, it was known for irrigation wells.
evidence.quote: By the 1950s, Codys Corner, now established under that name, was noted for its irrigation wells

evidence.claim: The Florida Geological Survey reported that artesian wells here, in St. Johns Park and in Bunnell supplied most of the groundwater pumped in the county.
evidence.quote: By the 1950s, Codys Corner, now established under that name, was noted for its irrigation wells, along with St. Johns Park and Bunnell. The Florida Geological Survey stated that most of the ground water pumped in the county came from artesian wells in these three areas.

evidence.claim: Preserve land now occupies much of the surrounding area, including the Relay Tract Conservation Easements just east of the crossroads.
evidence.quote: Much of the area around Codys Corner is dedicated preserve land, including the Relay Tract Conservation Easements just east of the community.

evidence.claim: At Dupont Road and State Road 11
evidence.quote: The community is at the intersection of Dupont Road and State Road 11

evidence.claim: Near Codys Corner, much of the surrounding land is dedicated to preserves.
evidence.quote: Much of the area around Codys Corner is dedicated preserve land

evidence.claim: The Old Brick Road was completed around 1917.
evidence.quote: completed around 1917

evidence.claim: His son John Joachim inherited the plantation in 1823 and managed it.
evidence.quote: At his death in 1823, his seventeen-year-old son, John Joachim Bulow inherited the property and managed it.

flags: FDOT gives 98 miles, while material maps 101.6. Use official 98-mile figure. This is a branching network; final paragraph and moments follow strip order Espanola, Flagler Beach/Bulow excursion, Codys Corner, not a claim of one continuous historic highway.
Cache gives little terrain, curvature or drive-time information. No such specifics added. The scenic designation date is distinct from Dixie Highway planning and construction.

Omitted current tagline’s claim of three centuries in use: FDOT makes a broad historical statement about the network, not continuous use of each modern alignment. No named Tribal source or detailed route history supports elaboration.

Bulow history is supported only by the cached encyclopedia article; the linked original 1839 document and park operator page are not cached. Retain the landmark and forced-labor history, without adding an agent or motive for its destruction or current operating hours.

Current Old Brick Road “starts here” wording replaced with the supported junction. Official cache supports walking, cycling and driving, but does not establish surface condition or restrictions for particular vehicles.
